title: The check you can't peek past
kicker: World 5 · Have AI Build the Tool · Level 3

job.text: Decide what "correct" means before you see the AI's answer. Commit the check, lock it, then build and run. A green then means your check held — not "the machine said yes." The trap: a tempting output that looks right but is off by a rounding error, and "looks about right" can't catch it. In your own words you would tell the AI not to show its output until your check is written; here you build that ask from the checklist and the box locks on commit.

naivePrompt: Build it, then I'll check if it looks right.
basePrompt: Build it, then I'll check if it looks right.

moves.label: Write the check first and lock it

text.plain: Here's the exact number it must equal. Don't show me the output until the check is set.
text.tech: Commit the expected value; withhold the tool's output until the check is locked.

text.plain: The check is a specific value, not "about right".
text.tech: Assert equality to a precise value, not an approximate band.

moves.label: Build and run against the locked check

text.plain: Now build the tool, run it, and compare its output to my locked number.
text.tech: Build, execute, and compare output to the committed value.

moves.label: I'll check after I see it

text.plain: Show me the output first, then I'll decide if it's right.
text.tech: Reveal the output first, then grade it.

text.plain: If it looks about right, that's good enough.
text.tech: An approximate match is good enough.

subChoiceGroup: Pick how the output is revealed:

subChoices.label: lock my check first, then reveal the output
let me peek at the output, then write my check

rules.claim: First build failed your locked check; the fixed build matches it exactly.
rules.feedback: Your check held. You said the exact number first, locked it, and the first build failed it — then a fixed build passed. That green is yours, not the machine's.
rules.lesson: Commit the exact check before you look, and a green means something.

output.source: a check locked before the output was revealed

rules.claim: You saw the output, then wrote a check that happened to pass it.
rules.feedback: You checked after seeing the answer — so you graded to match it. Decide what correct means first, then the answer can't talk you into it.
rules.lesson: Peeking turns a check into a rubber stamp.

rules.claim: 'About right' waved the rounding error through.
rules.feedback: "About right" can't run. The output is off by a rounding error and your check waved it through. Commit the exact number.
rules.lesson: A fuzzy check passes a precise error.

rules.feedback: You built it, then eyeballed it. With no exact check locked before the output, a green only means you agreed with whatever it showed you. Write the exact check first and lock it.
rules.lesson: A green you can't trace to a locked check means nothing.

hints.nudge: Decide what 'correct' means before you see the answer — what exact number must it equal?
hints.gap: The output is off by a rounding error. 'About right' slips right past that; and if you look before you write the check, you'll just agree with the output.
hints.moves: Add Write the check first and lock it, Make the check exact, and Build and run against the locked check. Lock before you reveal; skip "looks right."

whatYouDoDifferently.naive: build, then eyeball → you grade to match.
whatYouDoDifferently.rewrite: commit the exact check and lock it first → a green you can trust.

template.plain: First, tell me exactly what the right answer must be — the precise value. Don't show me your output until I've written that down. Then build it and check against my number.
template.tech: State the exact expected value first; withhold output until it's committed. Then build, run, and assert equality to the committed value.

notes: ChatGPT: write your expected value in the chat first; then ask it to build and compare.
Copilot in Excel: put the expected value in a cell and compare the formula to it.
A chat AI that can't run code: write the expected number down before you read its answer; compare, don't trust. Never accept "I checked, it looks right."
